title: Google Research unveils CoDaS, a multi-agent AI for prioritizing biomarkers from wearable sensor data
subtitle: The system runs a six-phase pipeline — profiling, hypothesis generation, parallel statistical and ML exploration, adversarial validation, literature review, and structured reporting — that mirrors the human biomarker discovery lifecycle.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Google Research published a blog post on August 21 introducing CoDaS — 'Co-Data-Scientist' — a multi-agent system for prioritizing candidate biomarkers in wearable sensor data. The pipeline runs six phases: data profiling, hypothesis generation, parallel statistical and machine-learning exploration, adversarial validation, deep literature research, and structured report generation, looped iteratively to mirror how a human research team would work a biomarker question. The work was led by MIT PhD student Yubin Kim during a Google internship, with Hamid Palangi and Daniel McDuff.

The design choice worth pausing on is the adversarial validation phase. Most 'AI for science' pipelines shipped in 2024 and 2025 stopped at hypothesis generation plus a single ML pass, which is where hallucinated correlations tend to slip through. CoDaS explicitly runs a separate agent whose job is to attack the candidate biomarkers the earlier phases produced — checking for confounders, dataset leakage, and effect sizes that will not survive replication — before the pipeline writes them into a report. That matches how a lab actually reviews a colleague's finding before publication.

Wearables are the right substrate for this. Watches, rings, and continuous glucose monitors capture heart-rate dynamics, sleep architecture, activity, and metabolic signals at population scale, which is exactly where subtle early-disease signatures live. The bottleneck for the last decade has been that the data is easy to collect and hard to interpret — most putative biomarkers do not replicate. A pipeline that automates the front half of that funnel and adversarially filters the output could turn wearable data from a health-tech pitch deck into an actual research instrument.

For learners in health-focused AI: read the paper for how the six phases hand off intermediate structured artifacts rather than free text. That is the pattern that makes multi-agent systems reproducible instead of impressive-looking-once. If you are building anything similar, the takeaway is that adversarial validation as a distinct phase — with its own agent, its own prompt, and its own success criterion — is what separates a demo from a tool a scientist would trust to run overnight.
